content:
Suspicious bulk orders of large quantities of second-hand books have led many booksellers to believe these books are being purchased on behalf of AI companies, allowing them to scan and use the content as training material without authors' consent or any payment.

An AirTag hidden among rare books sold as part of a bulk order seems to confirm this theory, as it ultimately ended up at an Amazon AI training facility...

Second-hand book dealers typically only receive orders for individual titles or small quantities of related books. However, for quite some time now, many booksellers have reported receiving bulk orders for second-hand books that appear to have no connection to each other whatsoever.

They suspect these books are being purchased by AI companies, then have their spines removed, before being scanned with high-speed scanning equipment to digitise the text for input into AI systems as training material.

Doing all this without the authors' consent and without paying any fees for using their works is, at the very least, unethical, but there has never been concrete evidence proving this is actually happening. A 404 Media investigation appears to have changed that.

The report itself is paywalled, but TNW has relayed the findings, noting that the tracking device used was an AirTag, and that employees at the facility confirmed what was taking place there.

Second-hand books are particularly valuable because anything published after 2022 could potentially contain text written or edited by AI systems; in other words, they may be using AI-generated output to train AI systems. Although publishing contracts almost universally explicitly prohibit authors from using AI-generated content, it is highly likely that some people will overlook this rule. As for self-published books, there is no effective regulation whatsoever.

Part of the problem is that intellectual property laws have yet to catch up with this practice. While doing this is likely illegal in the UK, a 2025 ruling in the US actually deemed it legal, claiming it constituted "transformative" use of copyrighted material.
